lesson.title: The Purest Glass Ever Made Rewired the World
lesson.summary: Fiber optic communication required both a theoretical insight, that sufficiently pure glass could carry light encoded information over long distances, and years of materials science to actually make glass that pure, and it eventually became the physical backbone of the internet, though not without a painful boom and bust cycle along the way.
lesson.body:
In 1966, Charles Kao and George Hockham, working at Standard Telecommunications Laboratories in the United Kingdom, published an analysis arguing that optical fibers could carry information over long distances using light, if the glass could be made pure enough to reduce signal loss to a specific, quantified threshold. At the time, the best available glass fiber lost far too much light over even short distances to be practical, so the paper was a theoretical target more than a working demonstration. Kao spent years afterward pushing the idea and the necessary materials science, work later recognized with a share of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The demonstrated breakthrough came in 1970, when researchers at Corning Glass Works, Robert Maurer, Donald Keck, and Peter Schultz, produced a fiber that met Kao's loss threshold, a genuine materials science achievement that required specialized purification techniques to remove trace impurities from the glass that would otherwise scatter or absorb the light signal. This is the same pattern seen in the transistor and the laser: a real, demonstrated result, in this case a physical spool of fiber that measurably worked, arriving years after the theoretical case was made, and still years before it would be practical to deploy at any meaningful scale.

Turning that laboratory fiber into a telecommunications network required combining it with the laser and later the semiconductor laser diode, discussed in the previous chapter, to actually generate the pulses of light the fiber would carry, plus the development of optical amplifiers, notably the erbium doped fiber amplifier in the late 1980s, which let a signal travel much further before needing to be electronically regenerated. Bell Labs and other telecommunications research organizations spent the 1970s and into the 1980s developing the systems engineering needed to deploy fiber commercially, and the first commercial fiber optic telephone systems went into service in the early 1980s, roughly fifteen years after Kao and Hockham's original paper.

Fiber optics is also a useful closing case because its investment history was not a smooth, triumphant line, which is a valuable corrective to end this book on. The rise of the internet in the 1990s drove an enormous wave of speculative investment in fiber optic infrastructure, with telecommunications companies laying vastly more fiber capacity than there was demand to fill, betting on internet traffic growth that would eventually arrive but had not yet. When that demand did not materialize fast enough, the bubble burst in the early 2000s, several major fiber and telecom companies collapsed or restructured, and a large amount of invested capital was lost even though the underlying technology was, and remains, completely real and enormously valuable. Today an overwhelming majority of the world's internet and long distance telephone traffic travels over fiber optic cable, including undersea cables that physically connect continents, and fiber is as close to invisible, load bearing infrastructure as any technology gets. The lesson to carry forward, and the one this book leaves you with, is that both things were true at once: fiber optics was, in the end, one of the truly transformative physics bets of the twentieth century, and a great many specific investors in it still lost money by overestimating how fast that transformation would arrive. Distinguishing a real technology from a speculative one, the skill this entire book has tried to build, tells you whether a bet is fundamentally sound. It does not, by itself, tell you when to place it, or how much of your portfolio it deserves. That second judgment, about timing and sizing rather than about reality, is the one no textbook can make for you, and is exactly why the risk-adjusted return and diversification principles from earlier chapters matter even when you are confident, correctly, that the physics is real.
